# 2 Maccabees Chapter 14 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 14 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_014_page_001.jpg

---

**14:1** Three years later, word reached Judas and his men that Demetrius son of Seleucus had sailed into the harbor of Tripolis with a strong army and a fleet

**14:2** and had seized the kingdom, after making away with Antiochus and his guardian Lysias.

**14:3** Now a certain Alcimus, who had been high priest and had deliberately defiled himself at the time of the mingling with the Gentiles, realized that no means of safety remained for him and no further access to the holy altar;

**14:4** so he came to King Demetrius in the hundred and fifty-first year, bringing him a golden crown and a palm branch, and besides these some of the customary olive branches from the temple. On that day he kept silent.

**14:5** But he found a suitable moment for his mad scheme: called into Demetrius's council and questioned about the attitude and purposes of the Jews, he answered:

**14:6** "Those among the Jews who are called Hasideans, whose leader is Judas Maccabeus, are maintaining a state of war and stirring up sedition, and will not let the kingdom have peace.

**14:7** Therefore, robbed of my ancestral dignity — I mean the high priesthood — I have now come here,

**14:8** first out of genuine concern for the king's interests, and second out of regard for my own fellow citizens; for because of the folly of the men I mentioned, our whole nation is in serious trouble.

**14:9** I urge you, therefore, O king, having acquainted yourself with all this, to take thought for our country and for our nation, which is beset on every side, in accordance with the gracious goodwill you show to all.

**14:10** For as long as Judas is alive, peace for the government is impossible."

**14:11** When he had said this, the rest of the king's friends, who were hostile to Judas, quickly inflamed Demetrius further.

**14:12** Immediately he appointed Nicanor, who had commanded the elephants, as governor of Judea, and sent him off

**14:13** with orders to kill Judas, disperse his supporters, and install Alcimus as high priest of the great temple.

**14:14** The Gentiles throughout Judea who had previously fled from Judas began flocking to Nicanor, thinking that the misfortunes and calamities of the Jews would serve their own interests.

**14:15** When the Jews heard of Nicanor's advance and the gathering of the Gentiles, they threw earth on their heads and entreated him who had established his people for ever and who always upholds his inheritance with his appearing.

**14:16** At the command of their leader, they moved out at once and met the enemy at a village called Dessau.

**14:17** Simon, the brother of Judas, had engaged Nicanor but suffered a temporary reverse because of the unexpected arrival of the enemy.

**14:18** Nevertheless, Nicanor, hearing of the valor of Judas and his men and their bravery in battle for their fatherland, shrank from settling the matter by bloodshed.

**14:19** So he sent Posidonius, Theodotus, and Mattathias to negotiate and exchange pledges of friendship.

**14:20** When the terms had been fully deliberated upon, and the leader had laid them before the multitude, and agreement had been reached, they consented to the covenant.

**14:21** They set a day on which to meet privately. A litter was brought forward from each side; chairs of state were placed.

**14:22** Judas had armed men stationed at strategic points as a precaution against any sudden treachery on the enemy's part. The conference was held in a proper manner.

**14:23** Nicanor remained in Jerusalem and did nothing irregular, but dispersed the crowds of people that had attached themselves to him.

**14:24** He kept Judas always at his side and was genuinely attached to the man.

**14:25** He urged him to marry and have children; Judas married, settled into a normal life, and shared in the common lot of men.

**14:26** But Alcimus, observing their goodwill for each other and taking hold of the agreements they had made, went to Demetrius and told him that Nicanor was being disloyal to the government, for he had appointed as his successor in Jewish affairs Judas, the man who was plotting against the kingdom.

**14:27** The king was provoked, and infuriated by the slanders of this most wicked man, wrote to Nicanor declaring that he was displeased with the agreements and ordering him to send Maccabeus to Antioch as a prisoner without delay.

**14:28** When this reached Nicanor, he was troubled and deeply grieved that he would have to annul their agreements when the man had done no wrong.

**14:29** But since it was impossible for him to go against the king's orders, he watched for an opportunity to carry out the command by some stratagem.

**14:30** Maccabeus, noticing that Nicanor was growing colder toward him and behaving more abruptly than usual in their meetings, concluded that this coldness betokened nothing good; so he gathered a considerable number of his men and went into hiding from Nicanor.

**14:31** When Nicanor recognized that the man had cleverly outwitted him, he went to the great and holy temple while the priests were offering the daily sacrifices and ordered them to surrender the man.

**14:32** When they declared on oath that they did not know where the man he sought could be found,

**14:33** he stretched out his right hand toward the sanctuary and swore this oath: "If you do not deliver Judas to me as a prisoner, I will raze this shrine of God to the ground and demolish the altar, and I will erect here a splendid temple to Dionysus."

**14:34** With that he departed. The priests, however, stretched out their hands toward heaven and called on him who always fights for our nation, saying:

**14:35** "You, O Lord of all, who stand in need of nothing, were pleased to have a temple for your habitation among us.

**14:36** So now, O holy Lord of all holiness, keep undefiled to all ages this house that has so recently been purified."

**14:37** One Razis, an elder of Jerusalem, was denounced to Nicanor — a man who loved his compatriots and was held in high esteem, a man called father of the Jews on account of his goodwill toward them.

**14:38** For in the earlier times of separation, when there was no intermingling, he had been accused of Judaism and had devoted body and soul with complete earnestness to Judaism.

**14:39** Nicanor, wishing to make his hostility to the Jews plain for all to see, sent more than five hundred soldiers to arrest him;

**14:40** for he thought that by seizing him he would strike a great blow to the Jews.

**14:41** Now when the troops were on the point of taking the tower and were forcing the door of the courtyard and had called for fire to be brought to burn the doors, being surrounded on all sides, Razis fell upon his own sword,

**14:42** choosing to die nobly rather than fall into the hands of sinners and suffer treatment unworthy of his noble birth.

**14:43** In his haste and the press of the moment, he missed his stroke; and while the crowd was pouring in through the doors, he ran up boldly to the wall and threw himself down bravely upon the crowd.

**14:44** But when they quickly drew back, he fell in the middle of the empty space.

**14:45** Still breathing, and inflamed with spirit, he raised himself; and though blood was streaming from his wounds in great gushes, he ran through the crowd. Then, standing on a sheer rock,

**14:46** now entirely drained of blood, he tore out his entrails and hurled them with both hands at the crowd. And calling upon the Lord of life and spirit to restore them to him again, he died in this manner.
